chapters.file: ch02 - Doctor Who and Philosophy.md
ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy.md
ch04 - Title Page.md
ch05 - We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!.md
ch06 - EPISODE 1 - I’m the Doctor. Who.md
ch07 - A Dead End.md
chapters.relation: Patrick Stokes uses the Doctor's regeneration and the multi-Doctor stories ("The Five Doctors," "The Caves of Androzani") to test theories of personal identity. He runs Locke's memory criterion against Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's Branch-Line teleportation case (a Gallifrey-to-Skaro replica), Nozick's Closest Continuer schema applied to the Valeyard, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity, showing each fails to explain regeneration. He gestures that identity may lie in a subjective self-appropriation, the Doctor taking ownership of his incarnations.

chapters.file: ch08 - Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann uses regeneration and dozens of Doctor Who transformations (doubles like the Abbot of Amboise, disembodied brains, transmats, Eldrad's body-hopping, Cassandra's possession) as hypotheticals to test criteria for personal identity. He shows bodily identity, spatiotemporal continuity of the body, the memory criterion (undercut by Donna and John Smith cases), and psychological/personality similarity each face counterexamples, deliberately leaving the question open so readers judge for themselves.

chapters.file: ch09 - What’s Persistence Without Identity.md
chapters.relation: Richard Hanley asks what counts as personal survival for a Time Lord, distinguishing body, mind, and soul theories. Using the Tenth Doctor's "every single cell" regeneration, the severed hand grown into a Doctor in "Journey's End," John Smith's Chameleon-Arch amnesia, and Jackson Lake's infostamp fugue, he argues bodily and soul continuity fail and defends a neo-Lockean mental-continuity criterion refined by Nozick's closest-continuer schema, concluding with Parfit that persistence may not be what matters in survival.

chapters.file: ch10 - I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think.md
chapters.relation: David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.

chapters.file: ch11 - EPISODE 2 - Wibbly-Wobbly, Timey-Wimey . . . Stuff.md
ch12 - We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel.md
chapters.relation: Peter Worley finishes the Doctor's "wibbly-wobbly" speech from "Blink" by distinguishing empirical from logical possibility (via a fictional chat with Leonardo about a round-square) and asking whether time travel is coherent. Using "The Edge of Destruction," "The Aztecs," "The Visitation," and "Turn Left," he deploys David Lewis's external-versus-personal time distinction and Lewis's rule that a time traveler's acts must be the very events that made history, then treats the Doctor and Lewis as "actualists" about possible worlds to dissolve grandfather-style paradoxes and time loops.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!.md
chapters.relation: Philip Goff asks whether Daleks could travel back and stop the pyramids being built, arguing the answer turns on one's theory of time. He shows presentism forbids travel to a non-existent past and eternalism permits travel but forbids changing a static block, then defends the growing-block theory (past and present real, future not) as a middle way that lets time travelers genuinely alter history. He works out how a new pyramid-less history advances at the same rate as the present, never overwriting it, and distinguishes concrete from abstract past existence to keep historical records true.

chapters.file: ch14 - Prognosis.md
chapters.relation: William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.

chapters.file: ch15 - This Is the Age of Steel.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.

chapters.file: ch16 - They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too.md
chapters.relation: Bonnie Green and Chris Willmott use the Daleks' human-factor experiments ("The Evil of the Daleks," "Dalek," "Daleks in Manhattan") to lay out the philosophy-of-biology "species problem": are species natural kinds, individuals, or sets? They trace essentialism from an Aristotelian God-given essence through Darwin's overthrow of it to modern genetic essentialism (the humanizing Dalek DNA), then use the Dalek/Thal split to survey biological species concepts and monism versus pluralism. They close with personhood and Peter Singer's speciesism, asking whether human-Dalek Sec would deserve rights.

chapters.file: ch17 - Doomed to Be Perceived.md
chapters.relation: Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.

chapters.file: ch18 - Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites.md
chapters.relation: Simon Hewitt uses the Carrionites, who wield words instead of numbers, to ask whether science can be done without mathematics, a question in the philosophy of mathematics about mathematical Platonism (numbers existing outside space and time). He lays out the Quinean indispensability argument, then reviews Hartry Field's number-free Newtonian gravity and Mark Balaguer's attempt on Quantum Mechanics as "Carrionite physics," noting both fall short. He closes arguing that even if numbers were dispensable for science, our knowledge of mathematical truths still suggests numbers exist.

chapters.file: ch19 - EPISODE 3 - It’s a Different Morality. Get Used to It, or Go Home!.md
ch20 - “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler.md
chapters.relation: Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.

chapters.file: ch21 - A Better Way of Living Your Life.md
chapters.relation: Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.

chapters.file: ch22 - Toward Caring.md
chapters.relation: J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.

chapters.file: ch23 - Allons-y into the Starry Heavens.md
chapters.relation: Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Dalek Within.md
chapters.relation: Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.

chapters.file: ch25 - Why the Doctor Is So Special.md
chapters.relation: Sarah Honeychurch and Niall Barr argue Daleks and Cybermen will never beat humanity because they are speciesist, judging worth solely by logic and resemblance. Using Peter Singer's animal-liberation account of speciesism (and Ryder's coinage), they claim the capacity to feel pain and empathy grounds moral consideration, and that Martha Nussbaum's and Aristotle's view of emotions as trainable judgments makes feeling essential to good moral reasoning. The humanized Daleks (the "Dalek" who absorbs Rose's DNA, Dalek Sec) show emotion's transformative power, and the Doctor's empathy, unlike other Time Lords, is why he succeeds.

chapters.file: ch26 - Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign.md
chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.
